panels:
Before DNS, the browser parses the URL (scheme, host, port, path, query, fragment; the fragment never leaves the browser) and checks HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security): a domain on the preload list or with a cached Strict-Transport-Security header is upgraded to https:// before any packet is sent. It may also reuse a warm connection from its pool, skipping DNS, TCP and TLS entirely, which is why second visits feel faster.

An HTTPS DNS record can advertise HTTP/3 support, so the browser may race QUIC against TCP (Happy Eyeballs also races IPv6 against IPv4). After the HTML arrives, the preload scanner discovers CSS, scripts and images early; CSS and synchronous scripts block rendering, so build the DOM and CSSOM, compute layout, then paint. Interviewers like candidates who mention caches at every layer: browser, OS, resolver, CDN, and HTTP caching via Cache-Control and ETag.

Every HTTP version keeps the same semantics: methods, status codes, headers and bodies, standardized in RFC 9110. Only the wire format changes: HTTP/1.1 is text with CRLF line endings, while HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 encode the same fields as binary frames with pseudo-headers such as :method and :path. The Host header (:authority in HTTP/2+) is mandatory because one IP address commonly serves many sites.

The body length is given by Content-Length or by chunked transfer encoding in HTTP/1.1; mismatches between proxies interpreting these differently cause request-smuggling bugs. Statelessness means the server needs no memory of previous requests to interpret this one, which lets load balancers send consecutive requests to different machines. State still exists, but it lives in cookies, tokens or a database. Content negotiation (Accept, Accept-Language, Accept-Encoding) lets the same URL return JSON or HTML, English or French, gzip or brotli.

Safe and idempotent are about intended semantics, not what your code happens to do. Safe methods should not change server state, so browsers, crawlers and caches may call them freely. Idempotent means N identical requests leave the same server state as one; responses may differ (a second DELETE can return 404) and side effects like logging are fine. PUT and DELETE are idempotent, POST is not, and PATCH is not guaranteed: an operation like 'append item' applied twice differs from once.

Idempotency matters because networks fail ambiguously: after a timeout the client cannot know whether the server acted. Payment APIs accept an Idempotency-Key header; the server stores key -> result and replays the stored response on retry, rejecting the same key with a different body. Retries should use exponential backoff with jitter. Caching follows a related rule: GET responses are cacheable by default when headers allow, POST responses almost never.

Some codes deserve precision. 301 and 308 are permanent redirects, 302 and 307 temporary; 307 and 308 guarantee the method and body are preserved, while browsers historically turn a redirected POST into GET for 301/302. 303 See Other deliberately switches to GET, the classic post-redirect-get pattern. 304 Not Modified answers a conditional request (If-None-Match with an ETag, or If-Modified-Since) and carries no body.

On the client side: 400 malformed request, 401 unauthenticated (must send WWW-Authenticate), 403 authenticated but forbidden, 404 not found (sometimes used instead of 403 to hide that a resource exists), 409 conflict, 422 validation failure, 429 rate limited with a Retry-After header. On the server side: 500 generic bug, 502 a gateway got a bad upstream response, 503 overloaded or in maintenance, 504 a gateway timed out waiting upstream. Retry 503/504 and 429 with backoff; do not blindly retry 4xx.

Cookie attributes are the security model. HttpOnly hides the cookie from JavaScript, limiting XSS token theft. Secure sends it only over HTTPS. SameSite=Lax (Chromium's default when the attribute is unset) withholds it on cross-site subrequests and cross-site POSTs but sends it on top-level navigations; Strict withholds it on all cross-site requests; None requires Secure and is needed for embedded third-party contexts. Domain widens scope to subdomains, and Path narrows it. The __Host- prefix forces Secure, Path=/ and no Domain.

Server-side sessions store an opaque random ID in the cookie and the data in Redis or a database: easy to revoke, but a shared store is required. Stateless tokens put signed claims in the cookie or an Authorization: Bearer header: no lookup, but hard to revoke before expiry. Rotate the session ID at login to prevent session fixation, and keep cookies small since they ride on every request.

In TLS 1.3 the client guesses the key-exchange group (usually X25519, increasingly the hybrid X25519MLKEM768 for post-quantum protection) and sends its key share in ClientHello. The server answers with its share, and everything after ServerHello is already encrypted, including the certificate. Both sides derive keys with HKDF; CertificateVerify proves the server holds the private key, and Finished messages authenticate the whole transcript. Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman gives forward secrecy: stealing the server's long-term key later cannot decrypt recorded sessions.

The client validates the certificate chain up to a trusted root CA, checks the hostname against the Subject Alternative Name, and checks expiry. SNI (Server Name Indication) reveals the hostname in clear text unless Encrypted Client Hello is used. Session resumption enables 0-RTT early data, but 0-RTT requests can be replayed, so servers should accept only idempotent requests that way. TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are deprecated.

HTTP/1.1 supports keep-alive and pipelining, but pipelining was unusable in practice because responses must come back in order, so one slow response blocks the rest. Browsers worked around this with about six parallel connections per origin, plus domain sharding and sprite sheets. HTTP/2 multiplexes interleaved frames from many streams over one connection and compresses headers with HPACK. Its weakness is TCP: one lost segment stalls delivery of every stream until retransmission.

HTTP/3 maps streams onto QUIC, which runs over UDP and implements reliability per stream inside user space, with TLS 1.3 built in. A new connection needs one round trip (zero on resumption) instead of TCP plus TLS. Connection IDs let a session survive a switch from Wi-Fi to cellular. Costs: UDP is sometimes blocked or throttled, so clients fall back to HTTP/2, and QUIC's user-space processing costs more CPU. HTTP/2 server push was removed by major browsers; 103 Early Hints replaces it.

More traps interviewers probe. Using GET for actions (GET /delete?id=5) lets link prefetchers and crawlers trigger them and leaks parameters into logs, browser history and Referer headers. Never put secrets or personal data in query strings. Returning 200 with an error message in the body breaks monitoring, caches and client retry logic; use accurate status codes.

CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is not a server security control: it only tells browsers which cross-origin JavaScript may read responses, and non-browser clients ignore it. Caching mistakes are common: a personalized response without Cache-Control: private or Vary can be served to other users by a CDN. Timeouts need to be set at every hop; a client timeout longer than the load balancer's produces confusing 504s. For the PUT retry quiz, note the subtlety: PUT is idempotent only if it sends the full replacement state, not a relative change like 'add one'.
swe-foundations-01.further: Read RFC 9110 (HTTP semantics) for the precise meaning of methods and status codes, and RFC 9111 for caching with Cache-Control, ETag and Vary. Next, study REST resource design versus RPC styles like gRPC and GraphQL, CDN behavior and cache keys, CORS preflight requests, and WebSockets or Server-Sent Events for server-to-client streaming. For performance, learn Core Web Vitals and how waterfall charts in browser dev tools reveal DNS, connect, TLS and time-to-first-byte phases. Post-quantum TLS key exchange is a current deployment topic worth tracking.

panels:
The TCP/IP model is what the internet actually runs; the OSI model is a teaching and vocabulary tool. Engineers still say 'layer 4 load balancer' (routes by IP and port) versus 'layer 7 load balancer' (routes by HTTP path or header), and 'layer 2' for switching within a LAN (local area network) using MAC addresses, while 'layer 3' routers forward by IP.

Encapsulation adds overhead at every layer: an Ethernet frame carries at most 1500 bytes of payload (the MTU, maximum transmission unit), of which IPv4 and TCP headers take at least 40, leaving an MSS (maximum segment size) of 1460. Tunnels and VPNs add headers and shrink the usable size; if Path MTU Discovery is broken because ICMP is filtered, large packets silently vanish while small ones work, a classic hard-to-debug failure. Real protocols blur layers: TLS sits between transport and application, and QUIC reimplements transport inside the application over UDP.

IPv4 has about 4.3 billion addresses, long exhausted, which is why NAT and address markets exist. IPv6 uses 128 bits written as eight hex groups; leading zeros drop and one run of zero groups becomes ::, so 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001 is 2001:db8::1. Special addresses: 127.0.0.1 and ::1 are loopback, 169.254.0.0/16 is link-local (often meaning DHCP failed), and 192.0.2.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24 and 203.0.113.0/24 are reserved for documentation.

Ports 0-1023 are well-known and need privileges to bind on most systems; 1024-49151 are registered; 49152-65535 are the ephemeral range clients use for outgoing connections (Linux defaults to 32768-60999). A TCP connection is identified by the 5-tuple: protocol, source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port. That is why one server port 443 can hold millions of connections, and why a single client can exhaust ephemeral ports when opening many short connections to the same destination.

Mask arithmetic: /n fixes n leading bits, leaving 2^(32-n) addresses. /24 = 256, /26 = 64, /28 = 16, /32 = one host; /0 means everything. Traditionally the first address is the network ID and the last is broadcast, so a /24 has 254 usable hosts; cloud providers reserve more, for example AWS reserves 5 per subnet, so a /28 gives 11 usable addresses.

To test membership, AND the address with the mask: 10.0.1.77 AND 255.255.255.0 = 10.0.1.0, so it is inside 10.0.1.0/24. Routers pick the most specific matching route (longest prefix match), which is how a /24 can override a /16. Plan cloud networks carefully: VPCs (virtual private clouds) that will be peered or joined by VPN must not overlap, and starting every environment at 10.0.0.0/16 is a common regret. Carrier-grade NAT uses 100.64.0.0/10, which can collide with internal ranges too.

TCP gives an ordered, reliable byte stream with no message boundaries, so applications must frame their own messages (length prefixes or delimiters). Sequence numbers count bytes, ACKs are cumulative, lost segments are retransmitted after a timeout or three duplicate ACKs, flow control uses the receiver's advertised window, and congestion control (CUBIC, BBR) probes for bandwidth. Head-of-line blocking follows: one lost segment holds back everything behind it.

The handshake exchanges random initial sequence numbers, which defeats spoofed or stale segments; SYN cookies let servers survive SYN floods without storing state. Closing uses FIN/ACK in each direction, and the side that closes first sits in TIME_WAIT for twice the maximum segment lifetime. UDP adds only ports, length and a checksum to IP: messages may be lost, duplicated or reordered, but there is no handshake and no head-of-line blocking. That is why DNS, real-time media and QUIC build exactly the reliability they need on top of UDP.

A stub resolver on your machine asks a recursive resolver (your ISP's, the corporate one, or a public one) to do the work. On a cold cache, the recursive resolver asks a root server where .com lives, asks the .com TLD servers where example.com's nameservers live, then asks the authoritative server for the record. Every answer is cached by its TTL, so most lookups never reach the root. Negative answers (NXDOMAIN) are cached too, which is why a typo'd record can keep 'not existing' after you fix it.

A CNAME cannot sit at the zone apex (example.com itself) alongside other records, hence provider-specific ALIAS/ANAME records. DNS mostly uses UDP port 53 and falls back to TCP for large responses and zone transfers. DNSSEC signs records to prevent spoofing; DNS over HTTPS and DNS over TLS encrypt queries for privacy. Lower TTLs to 60-300 seconds before a migration, then raise them afterwards.

NAT was invented to stretch IPv4. A home router performs PAT (port address translation): many private hosts share one public IP, distinguished by rewritten source ports, with a mapping table entry per flow that expires after idle time. That expiry is why long-lived idle connections die and why apps send keepalives. Carrier-grade NAT adds a second layer at the ISP, so even your router lacks a public address.

NAT is not a firewall, even though it blocks unsolicited inbound traffic as a side effect; a real firewall is still needed. It breaks end-to-end connectivity, so peer-to-peer apps use STUN to discover their public mapping, attempt hole punching, and fall back to relaying through TURN servers (the ICE framework, used by WebRTC). In cloud networks, a NAT gateway gives private subnets outbound internet access without exposing them inbound. IPv6 has enough addresses that NAT is unnecessary, though firewalls remain.

Work bottom-up and isolate one layer at a time. ping proves IP reachability only if ICMP is allowed; mtr combines ping and traceroute into a live per-hop loss view. traceroute sends probes with increasing TTL (time to live) and lists the routers that report 'time exceeded'; asterisks often just mean a router does not answer, not a failure. Loss that appears at one hop and disappears at later hops is usually rate-limited ICMP, not real loss.

dig shows the full answer, TTLs and which server replied; dig @1.1.1.1 example.com queries a specific resolver and dig +trace walks root -> TLD -> authoritative yourself. curl -v prints DNS resolution, connect, TLS handshake and headers; curl -w '%{time_connect} %{time_starttransfer}' splits the timing; curl --resolve forces an IP to test a server before DNS changes. For the transport layer, nc -vz host 5432 tests whether a port is open, ss -tlnp lists listening sockets, and tcpdump captures packets.

Other classic traps. 'Connection refused' means a host answered with RST: nothing listens on that port. A timeout usually means a firewall silently dropped the packets or the route is wrong. Distinguishing the two halves the search space. A service bound to 127.0.0.1 inside a container is unreachable from the host even with ports published; bind 0.0.0.0 there and restrict exposure at the network level.

DNS changes 'not working' are usually caching at the browser, OS, resolver or a JVM that caches lookups forever. MTU black holes show up as small requests succeeding and large ones hanging, often over VPNs. Ephemeral port exhaustion and many TIME_WAIT sockets appear under high connection churn; connection pooling fixes both. For the /28 quiz, remember the difference between total addresses (16) and usable hosts (14 traditionally, 11 in AWS). Always check whether a symptom is per-host, per-network or per-name before changing anything.
swe-foundations-02.further: Next, learn how load balancers differ at layer 4 and layer 7, how CDNs and anycast route users to the nearest edge, and how BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) ties autonomous networks together and occasionally breaks the internet. Study TCP congestion control (CUBIC versus BBR), the QUIC protocol, and IPv6 deployment. For cloud work, practice VPC design with route tables, security groups and NAT gateways. Wireshark and tcpdump are the tools that turn networking theory into something you can see packet by packet.

panels:
Paths are absolute (/var/log) or relative to the current directory; . is here, .. is the parent, ~ expands to your home directory and cd - jumps back to the previous directory. ls -la shows hidden dotfiles plus permissions, owner, size and modification time; ls -lh makes sizes human-readable, and du -sh * shows what is eating disk space while df -h shows free space per filesystem.

rm has no undo: deletion unlinks the name, and the data is reclaimed once no process holds the file open. That last detail explains a classic puzzle: deleting a huge log does not free space while a process still writes to it (find it with lsof +L1, then restart or truncate with : > file). mv within one filesystem is an instant rename; across filesystems it is copy-then-delete. tail -f follows a growing file; tail -F also survives log rotation. less is better than cat for large files since it does not load everything and supports / search.

Each file has an owner, a group and nine permission bits. For directories the bits mean something different: r lists names, w creates or deletes entries, and x lets you enter and traverse it. So deleting a file needs write permission on the directory, not on the file, and a directory with r but no x lets you see names but not open anything.

The umask removes bits from newly created files: the common 022 turns the default 666 into 644 for files and 777 into 755 for directories. Special bits form a leading fourth digit: setuid (4) runs a program as its owner (passwd uses it), setgid (2) on a directory makes new files inherit its group, and sticky (1) on /tmp stops users from deleting each other's files, so chmod 1777 /tmp. chown user:group file changes ownership and normally needs root. SSH refuses private keys readable by others, so chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.

Every process starts with three file descriptors: 0 stdin, 1 stdout, 2 stderr. Redirections are processed left to right, so order matters: cmd > out.txt 2>&1 sends both to the file, while cmd 2>&1 > out.txt sends stderr to the terminal because it copied stdout before stdout moved. Bash also offers &> file as shorthand. 2>/dev/null discards errors.

Pipe stages run concurrently, connected by kernel buffers (64 KB by default on Linux), so a slow consumer applies backpressure to the producer. A pipeline's exit status is the last command's, which hides failures earlier in the chain; set -o pipefail in scripts fixes this, usually alongside set -eu. tee writes to a file and passes data through. Process substitution, diff <(sort a) <(sort b), treats a command's output as a file. Here-documents (<<EOF) feed multi-line input. xargs turns lines into arguments: find . -name '*.tmp' -print0 | xargs -0 rm handles spaces in names.

grep uses basic regular expressions by default; -E enables extended syntax, -i ignores case, -v inverts, -l lists only matching files, -c counts, and -w matches whole words. ripgrep (rg) is a faster modern alternative that respects .gitignore. find walks the tree with predicates: -type f, -name with quoted globs (unquoted, the shell expands them first), -mtime +7 for modified more than seven days ago, -size +100M, and -exec cmd {} + to batch matches into one command. Test with -print before adding -delete.

sed applies scripts per line: s/old/new/g replaces all matches on a line, and -i edits in place, but GNU sed takes -i alone while macOS BSD sed needs -i ''. Any delimiter works, which helps with paths: s|/usr/local|/opt|g. awk splits each line into fields $1..$NF using whitespace by default (-F, for CSV-like input), runs pattern { action } rules, and has variables and END blocks, so awk '{s+=$3} END {print s}' sums a column. Neither parses real CSV with quoted commas; use a proper tool.

Each process has a PID, a parent PID, a user, and a state shown by ps: R running, S sleeping, D uninterruptible disk wait (cannot be killed even by SIGKILL until the I/O finishes), T stopped, Z zombie. A zombie has exited but its parent has not read its exit status; it uses no memory, and killing the parent lets init adopt and reap it. Load average counts runnable plus D-state processes, so high load can mean slow disks, not busy CPUs.

Signals: SIGTERM (15) is the polite default that programs can catch to shut down gracefully; SIGINT (2) comes from Ctrl+C; SIGHUP (1) often means 'reload config' for daemons; SIGKILL (9) and SIGSTOP cannot be caught or ignored. Ctrl+Z sends SIGTSTP, then bg resumes the job in the background and fg in the foreground; nohup or disown keeps a job alive after logout. Containers matter here: PID 1 does not get default signal handlers, so an app that ignores SIGTERM as PID 1 waits out the grace period before being killed.

VAR=value without export creates a shell variable that child processes do not see; export puts it in the environment that children inherit. A child can never change its parent's environment, which is why you source a script (. ./env.sh) rather than run it when it should set variables in your current shell. VAR=value cmd sets a variable for one command only. Always quote expansions, "$VAR", to prevent word splitting and glob expansion on spaces.

The shell searches PATH left to right and runs the first match; which or command -v shows which one wins. For SSH, prefer ed25519 keys protected by a passphrase and held in ssh-agent; ~/.ssh/config defines host aliases, users, keys and ProxyJump bastions. On first connection, verify the host key fingerprint; a changed key warning may mean a rebuilt server or an attack. -L does local port forwarding, -R remote forwarding, and -D a SOCKS proxy. scp works, but rsync -avz resumes, preserves metadata and copies only differences.

Walk the data through: access.log lines look like '203.0.113.7 - - [19/Oct/2026:10:00:01 +0000] "GET / HTTP/1.1" 200 512'. awk '{print $1}' emits one IP per line. uniq only collapses adjacent duplicates, which is why sort must come first. uniq -c prefixes counts such as '  412 203.0.113.7'. sort -rn sorts numerically in reverse, because plain sort is lexical and would put 9 after 10. head -5 keeps the top five.

Complexity: sort is O(n log n) and may spill to temp files for huge inputs, which is fine for gigabytes. A single-pass alternative uses an awk hash map: awk '{c[$1]++} END {for (ip in c) print c[ip], ip}' access.log | sort -rn | head -5, which is O(n) plus sorting only the distinct IPs. Variants interviewers like: count status codes with $9, filter 5xx first with awk '$9 >= 500', or watch live traffic with tail -f piped into grep --line-buffered.

The ${DIR:?} expansion makes the shell abort with an error if DIR is unset or empty, turning a catastrophic rm into a harmless failure. Pair it with set -euo pipefail at the top of scripts: -e exits on errors, -u treats unset variables as errors, pipefail surfaces failures in pipelines. Run ShellCheck on every script; it catches unquoted variables, useless cats and subtle bugs.

Permissions: 777 is a shortcut for 'I could not figure out ownership'; fix the owner or group instead, and use 600 for secrets. Do not pipe curl output from untrusted URLs straight into sh, and avoid running as root by default; use sudo for single commands. Parsing ls output breaks on spaces and newlines in names; use globs or find -print0. Editing a running script can change what bash executes mid-run because bash reads scripts incrementally. For chmod 640: 6 = 4+2 read and write, 4 = read only, 0 = nothing.
swe-foundations-03.further: Learn bash scripting properly: functions, arrays, exit codes, traps for cleanup (trap 'rm -f "$tmp"' EXIT) and ShellCheck. Then explore systemd units and journalctl for services, cron or systemd timers for scheduling, and observability tools like strace, lsof, htop and iostat for debugging misbehaving processes. jq is essential for JSON on the command line. Understanding namespaces and cgroups explains how containers are just isolated Linux processes, which is the bridge from shell skills to Docker and Kubernetes.

panels:
The OWASP Top 10 is an awareness document built from vulnerability data and community surveys, refreshed every few years (2017, 2021, 2025). Broken access control has held the top spot since 2021; the 2025 edition folds SSRF into it, elevates security misconfiguration, adds software supply chain failures (compromised dependencies, build systems and packages), and adds mishandling of exceptional conditions such as failing open on errors.

Use it as a checklist of categories, not a compliance standard; for verification depth, OWASP ASVS (Application Security Verification Standard) lists testable requirements. Interviewers probe whether you understand root causes rather than names: most entries reduce to mixing data with code, missing server-side checks, or trusting something the client controls. Defense in depth matters because single controls fail: input validation, output encoding, least privilege, secure defaults, dependency scanning and logging together. For LLM applications, OWASP maintains a separate Top 10 where prompt injection plays the role injection plays here.

Injection happens when untrusted input is interpreted as code by an interpreter: SQL, shell, LDAP, XPath, template engines or ORMs with raw fragments. With a parameterized query the statement is parsed first and the values are bound later, so input can never change the query's structure, regardless of quotes or encodings. Escaping by hand is fragile and differs per database and character set.

Placeholders cannot parameterize identifiers such as table names, column names or ORDER BY direction; map user choices to an allowlist of known values instead. ORMs are safe by default but expose raw query escape hatches that reintroduce the bug. Second-order injection stores malicious input safely, then a later code path concatenates it into a query. Shell injection: avoid shell=True and pass argument lists, as in subprocess.run(['convert', path, out]). Also limit blast radius: the application's database user should not own the schema or be able to drop tables.

XSS comes in three forms: stored (saved in the database and served to others), reflected (echoed from the request) and DOM-based (client-side code writes untrusted data into the page). The fix is context-aware output encoding: HTML body, attributes, URLs and JavaScript need different escaping. Frameworks like React escape by default, but dangerouslySetInnerHTML, href="javascript:..." and eval reopen the hole; sanitize rich HTML with a library like DOMPurify. A strict Content-Security-Policy with nonces stops injected scripts from running, and HttpOnly limits cookie theft.

CSRF works because browsers attach cookies to cross-site requests. SameSite=Lax blocks most cases; add synchronizer or double-submit tokens for sensitive forms, and never change state on GET. Token-based APIs using an Authorization header are not exposed to CSRF. SSRF lets attackers reach internal services or cloud metadata at 169.254.169.254; defend with destination allowlists, resolving and checking IPs after DNS (beware DNS rebinding and redirects), blocking private ranges, and IMDSv2-style session-token metadata.

Authentication establishes identity; authorization decides permissions for that identity on this resource. Authentication factors are something you know (password), have (security key, phone) or are (biometric). Passkeys (WebAuthn/FIDO2) use per-site public-key pairs, so they resist phishing and leave nothing reusable on the server; SMS codes are the weakest second factor because of SIM swapping.

Authorization models: RBAC (role-based access control), ABAC (attribute-based) and ReBAC (relationship-based, as in Google Zanzibar-style systems for 'can edit this doc'). The classic bug is IDOR (insecure direct object reference): the code fetches /invoices/1043 by ID without checking ownership. Random UUIDs make guessing harder but are not a control. Enforce checks in one central layer on the server, deny by default, and scope database queries by tenant (WHERE owner_id = ?). Hiding a button in the UI is never authorization. Write tests that try one user's token against another user's resources.

Password hashes must be slow to make offline guessing expensive. A modern GPU can compute billions of SHA-256 hashes per second, so fast hashes fall quickly to dictionary attacks. Argon2id is memory-hard, which defeats GPU and ASIC parallelism; OWASP guidance suggests parameters like 19 MiB of memory, 2 iterations and parallelism 1 as a minimum, tuned so hashing takes tens to hundreds of milliseconds on your servers. bcrypt is still acceptable with a cost of 10 or more, but it truncates input at 72 bytes. scrypt and PBKDF2 with high iteration counts are alternatives.

The salt is random per user and stored with the hash; it makes identical passwords hash differently and kills rainbow tables. A pepper is an additional secret kept outside the database, for example in an HSM. Rehash on login when parameters improve (argon2-cffi offers check_needs_rehash). Throttle login attempts, check new passwords against breached-password lists, and drop forced composition rules, which NIST guidance discourages.

OAuth 2.0 is an authorization delegation framework: the user lets an app act on their behalf with limited scopes, and the app never sees the password. Roles: resource owner (user), client (app), authorization server and resource server (API). The authorization code flow redirects the user to log in, returns a short-lived code to the redirect URI, and the client exchanges it for tokens over a back channel. PKCE binds the code to the client instance via a hashed code_verifier, defeating code interception; OAuth 2.1 makes PKCE mandatory and drops the implicit and password grants.

Access tokens are for APIs and should be short-lived; refresh tokens get new access tokens and should rotate on use. OAuth alone is not login: an access token says what the bearer may do, not who they are. OIDC adds the ID token (a JWT with sub, iss, aud, nonce) plus a userinfo endpoint. Validate the state parameter against CSRF and use exact redirect URI matching to avoid token theft.

A JWT is signed (JWS), not encrypted, unless it uses JWE; anyone can base64url-decode the payload, so never put secrets or sensitive personal data in it. Algorithm confusion attacks: accepting alg none, or verifying an RS256 token with HS256 using the public key as the HMAC secret, lets attackers forge tokens. Pin the algorithm and key per issuer, fetch public keys from a JWKS endpoint by kid, and validate exp, nbf, iss and aud with small clock skew.

Statelessness is both the benefit and the problem: a stolen token stays valid until expiry. Mitigations are short lifetimes (5-15 minutes), rotating refresh tokens with reuse detection, and a denylist for emergencies, which reintroduces state. Storing tokens in localStorage exposes them to any XSS; HttpOnly cookies avoid that but bring CSRF back into scope. For first-party web apps, plain server-side sessions are often simpler and safer than JWTs; JWTs shine for service-to-service calls and federated identity.

Secrets include API keys, database passwords, signing keys and TLS private keys. Keep them in a secrets manager (cloud KMS-backed stores, HashiCorp Vault and similar) with access control, audit logs and rotation. Prefer short-lived dynamic credentials and workload identity, such as cloud IAM roles or OIDC federation from CI, over long-lived static keys. Environment variables are common but can leak through crash dumps, debug pages, child processes and logs; mounted files or direct SDK fetches are tighter.

Once a secret is pushed, assume it is compromised within minutes, since bots scan public repositories continuously. Revoke and rotate first, then clean history with git filter-repo if needed; forks and caches may already hold copies. Prevent leaks with pre-commit secret scanners and push protection. Security logging should record authentication failures and authorization denials without logging the secrets or tokens themselves. The quiz case is IDOR: the fix is an ownership check on every object access, not hiding IDs.
swe-foundations-04.further: Go deeper with the OWASP Cheat Sheet Series and ASVS, then practice on deliberately vulnerable apps such as OWASP Juice Shop. Study threat modeling (STRIDE), security headers (CSP, HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options), CORS versus CSRF, and supply chain security: lockfiles, dependency scanning, SBOMs (software bills of materials), signed builds and SLSA levels. Learn WebAuthn and passkeys in detail, OAuth 2.1 and token binding ideas like DPoP, and how zero-trust architectures replace network perimeters with per-request identity checks.

panels:
Concurrency is a property of program structure: independent tasks whose execution can overlap in time. Parallelism is a property of execution: multiple tasks literally running at once on separate cores or machines. A single-core machine time-slices threads every few milliseconds, giving concurrency without parallelism; a GPU running one kernel across thousands of cores is parallelism with little concurrency in the structural sense.

The practical split is I/O-bound versus CPU-bound work. I/O-bound programs spend most time waiting on networks or disks, so concurrency alone (threads or async) gives big speedups. CPU-bound programs need parallelism, and Amdahl's law caps the gain: if 10% of the work is serial, the maximum speedup is 10x no matter how many cores you add. Interviewers also probe the cost side: context switches take microseconds, shared caches suffer contention, and more threads than cores often slows CPU-bound work down.

A process owns an address space, file descriptors and at least one thread; the OS isolates processes with virtual memory, so a bug in one cannot overwrite another. Communication goes through IPC: pipes, sockets, shared memory segments or message queues, and data usually must be serialized. Creating a process costs more: fork uses copy-on-write pages, but each process still has its own page tables and memory footprint.

Threads share heap, globals and file descriptors but each has its own stack (often 1-8 MB reserved) and registers. Shared memory makes communication free and bugs easy. An unhandled crash such as a segfault in one thread kills the whole process. Beyond OS threads, green threads and coroutines (Go goroutines, Java virtual threads since Java 21, Python asyncio tasks) are scheduled in user space, cost kilobytes instead of megabytes, and allow millions of concurrent tasks. Multiprocess designs trade overhead for isolation, which is why browsers put each site in its own process.

A data race is two threads accessing the same memory without synchronization where at least one writes. A race condition is broader: correctness depends on timing, even if each step is individually atomic. Check-then-act is the classic example: if not os.path.exists(f): create(f), or 'if balance >= amount: withdraw', where another thread acts between the check and the act. The same bug appears across processes and machines, such as two web servers both reading a stock of 1 and selling the last item twice.

Races are hard because they are nondeterministic: a test passes 999 times and fails under production load or on a different CPU. Compilers and CPUs also reorder memory operations, so without synchronization one thread may see another's writes late or out of order; memory models (Java, C++) define happens-before rules. Tools help: ThreadSanitizer for C, C++ and Go, go test -race, and stress tests that add random delays.

A mutex guarantees mutual exclusion and also memory visibility: changes made before unlock are visible to the next thread that locks. Always release in a finally block or with a context manager, since an exception while holding a lock blocks every other thread forever. Python's threading.Lock is not reentrant; a thread that locks it twice deadlocks itself, while RLock allows re-entry. Read-write locks allow many readers or one writer, and semaphores allow up to N holders, useful for capping concurrent connections.

Locks have costs: contention serializes threads, and holding a lock across I/O destroys throughput. Alternatives often scale better: atomic compare-and-swap operations for counters and lock-free structures, thread-safe queues so only one thread owns each piece of state (the producer-consumer pattern), immutable data shared freely, and the actor model or channels ('share memory by communicating', as Go puts it). Across machines, database transactions, row locks and optimistic concurrency with version numbers replace mutexes.

The four Coffman conditions (1971) are all necessary for deadlock, so preventing any one prevents it. Mutual exclusion is hard to remove for writable resources. Hold and wait can be broken by acquiring all locks at once or releasing held locks before requesting more. No preemption can be broken with try-lock plus timeout: on failure, release everything, back off and retry, at the risk of livelock where threads keep retrying in lockstep. Circular wait is broken by a global ordering, for example locking accounts in ascending ID order regardless of transfer direction.

Databases detect deadlocks with a wait-for graph and abort one transaction as the victim, so applications must retry failed transactions. Related failures: livelock (active but no progress) and starvation (one thread never gets the lock, fixed by fair locks). Diagnose hangs with thread dumps (jstack, py-spy dump, or Go's SIGQUIT dump), which show which thread holds which lock and what it is waiting for.

An event loop runs on one thread: it keeps a queue of ready callbacks or coroutines and asks the OS, via epoll, kqueue or IOCP, which sockets are ready. A coroutine runs until it hits await on something not ready, then yields so the loop can run others. Because switches happen only at await points, code between awaits cannot be interrupted by other tasks on the same loop, which removes many races, though state can still change across an await.

The cardinal rule is never block the loop: time.sleep, a synchronous HTTP client, a slow file read or a CPU-heavy loop stalls every task. Use async libraries, asyncio.sleep, and asyncio.to_thread or a process pool for blocking or CPU work. asyncio.gather runs tasks concurrently; TaskGroup (Python 3.11+) adds structured concurrency so failures cancel siblings. Calling an async function without await just creates an unawaited coroutine that never runs. Cap concurrency with a Semaphore so you do not open 10,000 sockets at once. Node.js uses the same model with a libuv thread pool behind it.

Why the lost updates happen: n += 1 compiles to load n, add 1, store n. If the interpreter switches threads between the load and the store, both threads store the same value and one increment disappears. In CPython the switch interval is 5 ms by default and recent versions switch less often inside such loops, so the bug may appear rarely; on a free-threaded build or in Java or C it shows up readily. Rarely is worse than always, because it escapes tests.

The with lock: statement acquires before the increment and releases afterwards, even on exceptions. Locking inside the loop is correct but slow because every iteration contends; a better design gives each thread a local counter and combines once at the end, needing one lock acquisition per thread instead of 100,000. For real counters use atomics (AtomicLong in Java, std::atomic in C++) or itertools.count, whose next() is atomic in CPython. Verify fixes by running many trials and asserting the exact total.

CPython's GIL lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time, which simplified reference counting and C-extension safety. Threads still help for I/O, because the GIL is released during blocking system calls, and NumPy and many C extensions release it during heavy computation. For pure-Python CPU work, threads give no speedup; use multiprocessing or concurrent.futures.ProcessPoolExecutor, paying the cost of pickling arguments and results.

PEP 703 added an optional free-threaded build (python3.13t); with Python 3.14 it became officially supported, though not the default, and some C extensions still need updates. Removing the GIL makes races more likely to surface, not less. The GIL never made compound operations atomic: += on shared data, check-then-act on dicts and iterating a list while another thread mutates it all need explicit synchronization. For the quiz, A->B in one thread and B->A in another creates circular wait; a fixed lock order removes it.
swe-foundations-05.further: Explore memory models and happens-before rules, lock-free data structures with compare-and-swap, and the ABA problem. Compare concurrency models across languages: Go goroutines and channels, Java virtual threads, Rust's ownership rules that prevent data races at compile time, and the actor model in Erlang and Akka. For distributed systems, study optimistic concurrency control, distributed locks and their pitfalls (fencing tokens), and idempotent message processing. 'The Little Book of Semaphores' offers classic synchronization puzzles such as dining philosophers.
